Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Stock Broker
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Fawn Response: become overly compliant when feeling threatened, Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Marisol Alvarez was 53 when she came for treatment, a married Latina stock broker who had spent most of her adult life moving briskly through crowded elevators, trading floors, client dinners, and late-evening walks back to parking garages without much thought about personal safety. The robbery happened on an ordinary weekday after work. She had left her office later than planned, still in her heels, carrying her laptop bag and talking herself through the next morning’s market opening as she crossed toward the garage a block from her building. A man stepped out fast from between two parked cars and closed the distance before she had time to react. What stayed with her was not only that he demanded her bag and wallet, but the abruptness of his body coming at her—his arm shooting forward, the sharp movement of his shoulders, the way his hand jerked toward her chest as if he might strike her if she hesitated. She remembered freezing and then immediately trying to placate him, her voice turning soft and apologetic as she told him he could take everything, that she was not going to cause trouble, that she was sorry. Even now she felt ashamed by how quickly she had become agreeable, but in those seconds it had felt like the only way to get out alive.

In the days afterward she expected to calm down once the police report was filed and her credit cards were replaced. Instead, what took root most strongly was the sense that the world had shown its true nature. She had come to believe that danger was not exceptional or limited to bad neighborhoods or bad luck; it was simply what the world was. She was also bitterly angry at how exposed she had been. The garage had poor lighting, there was no visible security presence, and when she tried to follow up after making her report, the responses felt perfunctory. She found herself dwelling on the people and systems that were supposed to keep ordinary working people safe and concluded that they had failed her completely. That thought carried a particular sting because she had done everything she thought a responsible person should do—worked hard, stayed alert, used a professional garage—and still no one had protected her.

Over the following months, her days narrowed around vigilance. At the office she could no longer simply step out of an elevator or walk across the lobby while reviewing numbers on her phone. She scanned constantly: who was near the revolving doors, who was standing too close, who moved too quickly. On the trading floor, if a colleague pushed back suddenly from a chair or reached across her desk without warning, her body snapped to attention before she could think. The sudden movements were especially potent; they carried the same electric jolt as the man stepping out in front of her. Ordinary sounds did it too. A dropped binder, a phone slammed onto a desk, a burst of laughter behind her—each one made her jump hard enough that coworkers started noticing. She laughed it off when she could, but inside she was flooded with fear and then anger at herself for seeming so rattled.

She also developed quiet routines she did not tell anyone about. Before leaving home, before entering the garage, before stepping out of her car, she silently repeated certain phrases in her head in a fixed order. If she got distracted, she started over. It made little logical sense to her, but she felt she had to do it properly, as if completing the sequence could keep another attack from finding her. The ritual gave her brief relief, though only briefly; once she was in motion again, she was back to checking reflections in glass doors, listening for footsteps, and tracking everyone’s hands.

At home, her husband noticed a different change. Marisol was not simply frightened; much of the time she felt hollow. She sat through dinner barely responding, unable to take in his concern or enjoy the small habits that had once anchored them. She described feeling dead inside, as if some internal switch had shut off. The combination of strong fear, flashes of horror, simmering anger, and this deadened absence left her feeling unlike herself. Her marriage became strained not through arguments so much as through withdrawal. She stopped agreeing to dinners out after work and avoided evening events with clients unless she absolutely had to go, which began to affect how she managed relationships in a profession built on confidence and access.

What finally brought her to seek help was a recent morning at work when a junior associate came up quickly behind her and waved a sheet of paper into her line of sight. Marisol recoiled so sharply that she knocked over her coffee and then, to her humiliation, heard herself speaking to him in the same overly careful, appeasing tone she had used during the robbery. The incident left her shaken for the rest of the day. She said she was tired of living as if threat were everywhere and tired of feeling empty in the middle of a life that, on paper, had been put back together. What frightened her most was the sense that she could no longer trust the world, other people, or even her own reactions. What she hoped for, though she said it cautiously, was to walk into her office, into a garage, into her own life, without bracing for disaster at every sound and sudden movement.
